Use lighter leaders and tidy knots – albacore often demand a more refined presentation than their size suggests.

When predators crash a bunker school, drop a live or chunk bait just off the edge of the mass, not into the centre of the chaos.

MEN.playful_bio_en: Daylight schooling filter feeder. Castnet territory — more bait than catch...
advice: Treat menhaden as a bait mission – you are stocking the livewell, not hunting a trophy.
Use sabiki-style rigs or small multi-hook bait strings around harbour mouths, bridges and obvious bunker schools.
Keep a slow trickle of mashed menhaden or oily groundbait going to hold the school under the boat.
Handle fish quickly and gently – lively, silver baits out-fish tired, red-eyed ones every time.
When predators crash a bunker school, drop a live or chunk bait just off the edge of the mass, not into the centre of the chaos.

Slow-troll or drift live baits or whole squid just above the bottom rather than dragging them into the rocks.
Vertical jigs and slow-pitch metals work well over marks – use long pauses and short lifts to imitate injured baitfish.
Step up leaders and knots; dentex hit hard and dive immediately for cover, so weak links get found quickly.

Use slim, fast lures – minnows, metals and soft plastics – and retrieve with sharp changes of pace.

Move until you find bites – if nothing happens in ten to fifteen minutes, slide a few steps along.

Target greenish, rolling surf rather than milky churn or flat, lifeless water.
Cast slightly along the beach with the longshore current so baits sweep naturally across feeding lanes.

Use small worm and crab baits on simple, light rigs that can move with the flow.

On big tides, fish the flood up onto mudflats and the ebb back off them.

scophthalmus-maximus.playful_bio_en: Dawn/dusk drifts along sandbank shoulders. Whole sandeel gets me every time...
advice: Focus on sandbanks, gullies and seams where tide funnels sandeels and small fish.

diplodus-vulgaris.playful_bio_en: Striped seabream that loves rocks and weed. Light tackle champion!
advice: Fish inshore rock patches, reef edges and broken ground where small seabream pick over weed and stones.
Scale down: fine hooks, light fluorocarbon and small baits get many more takes from wary fish.
Use tiny pieces of prawn, crab or shellfish and change baits often to keep scent levels high.
Float rigs or light running ledgers that let baits waft just above the bottom work better than heavy static leads.
On calm, clear days, step even lighter and keep noise and movement on the rocks to a minimum.

rhomboplites-aurorubens.playful_bio_en: Daytime and dusk over deep structure. Small cut baits and a moving tide — say no more...
advice: Look for mid water marks over deep reefs and ledges on the sounder rather than glued to the bottom.
Use lighter leaders and smaller hooks than for big red snapper to get more bites.
Drop multi hook rigs with small pieces of squid or fish and keep them just above the main structure.
Short lifts and drops often outfish big rod sweeps in deeper water.
If small fish dominate, move a little shallower or deeper along the same structure until you find better marks.

acanthocybium-solandri.playful_bio_en: Early morning offshore speedster. High-speed lures or livebaits — don't slow down...
advice: Work drop-offs, ledges and current edges where deep water pushes tight to the reef or island.
Troll fast with high-speed lures or rigged baits; wahoo often react to pace and direction changes.
Run lures at staggered depths and distances to cover different lanes in the wake.
Use wire or very tough fluorocarbon leaders – razor teeth and high speed find weak points fast.
After a strike, loop back across the same contour or colour change; packs often hold along specific lines.

advice: Whiting hunt in packs – once you find them, keep baits in the water and recast regularly.
Fish small, fresh baits on fine wire hooks for more positive bites and better hook-ups.

Use simple two- or three-hook rigs to search different levels just off the bottom.

advice: Target soft mud and sand flats in sheltered bays, estuaries and channels in the cooler months.
Fish small hooks and small baits – pieces of worm, clam or mussel get far more positive takes.

Chum lightly with crushed shellfish or chopped worm to hold fish in a small area.
Short drifts or even still fishing over a small patch of good bottom usually out-fish long wanderings.

advice: Work temperature breaks, current edges and bait-rich structure such as rigs, banks and weedlines.
Troll a spread of lures or baits at different distances and depths until you find the height fish are holding.

Match lure and leader size to the grade of fish and water clarity; go finer when the sea is flat and the sun is high.
Bleed and ice fish promptly if you plan to eat them – good handling dramatically improves eating quality.
